questions.stem: What does an electric current in a conductor produce?

options.text: a magnetic field around the conductor
options.explanation: Current is a source of magnetic field — the electromagnetism link.

options.text: a gravitational field around the conductor
options.explanation: Gravity is unrelated to current flow.
Copper stays non-magnetic; the effect is the field around it.

options.text: an electric field in circles around the wire
options.explanation: The circular pattern belongs to the magnetic field.

questions.stem: The magnetic field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are:

options.explanation: Parallel-line patterns belong to uniform gaps between poles.
The field wraps the wire in concentric rings.
Field lines run around, not along, the wire.

options.text: lines from the wire's ends like a bar magnet
options.explanation: A straight wire has no poles — the pattern is circular.

questions.stem: The current in a wire is reversed. What happens to the magnetic field around it?

options.text: the circles keep their direction but tighten
options.explanation: Direction flips; spacing depends on distance and current size.
Reversal changes direction, not field type.
Field direction follows the current direction.
A reversed current still produces a field.

questions.stem: The current is switched off. What remains of the wire's magnetic field?

options.explanation: Copper carries no permanent magnetism.
Switching off is not reversing.
Fields are not frozen into the space around copper.

options.text: nothing — the field exists only while current flows
options.explanation: Current is the source; no current, no field.

questions.stem: Which rule gives the direction of the field circles around a straight wire?

options.text: the right-hand grip rule — thumb along the current
options.explanation: Curled fingers give the circulation sense.
Left-hand rule is for forces on currents, not field direction around them.

options.text: the left-hand grip rule with thumb along the field
options.explanation: The grip rule is a right-hand rule, and the thumb follows the current.

options.text: trial and error with a stopwatch
options.explanation: Direction comes from the grip rule, not timing.

questions.stem: State what a current in a conductor produces.
questions.modelAnswer: A magnetic field is produced in the space around the conductor.

questions.stem: State the shape of the field lines around a straight current-carrying wire.
questions.modelAnswer: The field lines are circles centred on the wire.

questions.stem: Explain how the right-hand grip rule is used with a straight wire.
questions.modelAnswer: Grip an imagined wire with the right hand so the thumb points along the current direction; the curled fingers then show the circulation direction of the magnetic field circles around the wire. The rule works because the field's sense is fixed by the current's direction, and the hand geometry encodes that link.

questions.stem: A vertical wire carries current upwards. State the direction of the field seen from above, and predict the change if the current is doubled and then reversed.
questions.modelAnswer: Viewed from above, the field circles circulate anticlockwise by the grip rule with current flowing up. Doubling the current strengthens the field but keeps the anticlockwise sense; reversing the current makes the circles circulate clockwise instead.

questions.stem: What happens to the field around a wire when the current is increased?

options.explanation: Increasing a current does not reverse it.
Field strength scales with the current.
That inverts the current–strength link.

options.text: the field shape changes to straight lines
options.explanation: The circles remain circles; only strength changes.

questions.stem: Where is the field around a straight wire strongest?

options.explanation: The circular field is not uniform — it fades outward.
A straight wire has no end poles.
Strength falls with distance from the wire.
The field weakens with distance, so distant points are weak.

questions.stem: How do the field lines show the weakening of the field with distance?

options.text: the circles become squares far away
options.explanation: The shape stays circular; spacing changes.
Arrow length is not the encoding for strength here.

options.text: they do not — spacing never changes
options.explanation: Spacing is exactly how strength is shown.

options.text: the circles spread further apart with distance
options.explanation: Wider spacing encodes a weaker field.

questions.stem: Two wires carry currents of 1 A and 3 A. Their field circles at equal distances compare how?

options.text: the 3 A wire's field is stronger at that distance
options.explanation: Larger current, stronger field at the same place.

options.text: the 1 A wire's field is stronger
options.explanation: Strength grows with current, not the reverse.

options.text: the fields are equal at equal distances
options.explanation: Different currents give different strengths at the same distance.
Both currents produce fields.

questions.stem: A compass near a wire deflects strongly; doubling the distance makes the deflection small. What does this show?

options.text: the field reversed direction with distance
options.explanation: The sense of circulation is distance-independent.

options.text: the wire's field weakens with distance
options.explanation: Smaller deflection means a weaker field at the compass.
A working compass shows exactly this distance behaviour.

options.text: the current dropped when the compass moved
options.explanation: Moving the sensor cannot change the circuit current.

questions.stem: State the two factors that control the strength of the field around a current-carrying wire.
questions.modelAnswer: The size of the current and the distance from the wire.

questions.stem: State what happens to the field when the current is switched off.
questions.modelAnswer: The magnetic field disappears because it exists only while current flows.

questions.stem: Explain why the circles drawn around a wire are closest together near the wire itself.
questions.modelAnswer: Spacing encodes strength: the field around a current-carrying wire is strongest at the surface and weakens with distance, so the circles are drawn crowded near the wire and progressively wider apart further out. The drawing convention turns the strength falloff into visible geometry.

questions.stem: A technician wants the strongest possible field at a sensor fixed 5 cm from a wire, using a variable supply. State the adjustment and justify it.
questions.modelAnswer: Turn the supply up to the largest safe current: field strength around the wire grows with the current, so the maximum current gives the strongest field at the fixed 5 cm position. The distance cannot be changed — the sensor is fixed — so current is the available lever.
